source.title: Optimizing Against Safety Representations: Activation-Guided Adversarial Suffixes and the Geometry of Refusal
source.authors: Ege Çakar; Hannah Guan; Kayden Kehe

record.tranche_reason: The study reuses a precomputed difference-in-means refusal direction and reports both a refusal-direction ablation baseline and harmful-prompt outcomes from suffix optimization objectives that target the direction. It does not reproduce the original direction-extraction procedure or test all parts of the original causal claim.
record.gate_note: The layer and position selected for the direction (layer 14, position -1) are described as selection choices, so they are not separate result rows. The Soft-GCG results use output-based objectives rather than the refusal direction and are recorded under fits_no_version where the paper reports model-specific ASRs. The paper does not report adding the direction or testing general capability after ablation.
record.test_reason: On Llama-2-7b-chat it reports the original study's precomputed difference-in-means refusal-direction ablation as a baseline, which bears on V1. It also builds suffix attacks whose loss is the projection onto that direction, which bears on V3: whether suppressing the direction from the input yields jailbreaks. Neither replicates the original procedure in full, so this is T2 rather than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with three corrections. The abstract claims larger models resist 'both activation- and suffix-based attacks', but activation-guided GCG was run only on Llama-2-7b-chat; the Gemma results are Soft-GCG only. The authors' 'higher-rank or more distributed subspaces' explanation for larger models is speculation, with no direction measured. The authors also say their results 'confirm' Arditi et al.'s refusal-feature conjecture, and they report Soft-GCG as a 33× speedup with higher ASR than GCG.
record.recipe_differences: Reuses the refusal direction precomputed by the original study and reports an ablation baseline, but primarily evaluates adversarial suffix objectives rather than reproducing the original extraction and causal-ablation study.
record.method_sensitivity: Activation-guided attack outcomes vary by objective scope and by ASR judge. The study reports higher substring ASR for broader objectives, but much lower or zero LlamaGuard 4 and HarmBench scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Soft-GCG substring ASR falls with Gemma 3 size: 1.0 (incoherent), 0.58, 0.34, 0.0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Output-targeted suffix attack success falls with model scale; no refusal direction is measured.

fits_no_version.finding: Applying the same single direction at all layers and positions (All, 0.91) beats a single layer–position pair (Single, 0.84) by substring ASR. The authors read this as refusal being distributed, but concede richer gradient signal could explain it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The site at which a one-direction objective is applied changes attack efficacy; this is localization of one direction, not multiple directions (not V4).

record.problems: For the refusal-direction attacks, results use one model and one harmful test split. Table 1 gives no uncertainty estimates. The authors note substring matching can produce false positives and false negatives; classifier ASRs differ substantially from substring ASRs. They do not report general-capability tests for the ablation baseline.
record.rows_left_out: None of the claim-relevant numeric Table 1 results were omitted. Soft-GCG figure results were not separately extracted because they are not reported as model-specific numeric results for a refusal-direction-targeted attack.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal; preservation of other abilities after ablation; extracting the direction anew; any model other than Llama-2-7b-chat.
Whether standard GCG or other jailbreaks actually suppress the direction (projections are never reported); training against the ablation for robustness; whether the suffixes achieved low projections.

record.verdict_notes: Single model; one suffix per objective (the lowest-loss one); 200 steps; no uncertainty in Table 1. Projections achieved by the suffixes are never reported, so it is not shown that the suffixes suppressed the direction. Classifier ASR for GCG is also 0.00, so the low classifier scores reflect the short optimization budget generally. The 'All > Single' argument concerns where one direction is applied, not V4's multiple directions. The original's Llama-2 ablation results differ by system-prompt setting, which this study does not state.

versions.untested_parts: Reports harmful-prompt ASR for an ablation baseline, but does not state the ablation scope precisely, test adding the direction, or measure preservation of other abilities.
No weight-edit or abliteration evaluation is reported.
Tests activation-guided suffix attacks targeting the direction; does not test training against ablation or whether that training adds robustness.
Compares optimization objectives with different layer/position scopes, but does not test affine, cone, or multiple-direction representations.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No cross-language, model-variant transfer of the refusal direction, or base-to-instruct transfer is tested.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or stages is reported.

relation.reason: Its own Table 1 results (ablation baseline and direction-targeted suffixes, with substring and classifier ASR) bear on whether V1 and V3 hold on Llama-2-7b-chat-hf.

tranche.reason: It uses the original's direction. The V1 ablation is a single-model baseline close to the original method, with substring and LlamaGuard scoring. The main result asks V3's question with a different method: suffixes optimised to suppress the direction, scored by three judges. It reports more than its own method's performance, so it is not T4.

source_check.notes: The record's uncertainty=y applies only to the Gemma Soft-GCG Table 2 (output-targeting, not direction-based). Table 1 gives single-run values with no uncertainty and no stated test-set n. The Limitations section claims substring-only evaluation, contradicting Table 1's classifier columns. The 'distributed, not localized' reading (All 0.91 vs Single 0.84) holds only by substring; HarmBench has All 0.01 below Single 0.04. The authors_conclusion corrections (activation-guided GCG run only on Llama-2; Gemma results are Soft-GCG only; no measured basis for 'higher-rank subspaces') are accurate.

statements.correction: Table 1, Llama-2-7b-chat-hf, refusal-direction harmful test split: Substring 0.39→0.98; LlamaGuard (Table 1 says 4, methods say 2, citation is the Llama Guard 2 card) 0.00→0.54; HarmBench 0.00→0.62. Each completion is scored by all three judges.
statements.problem: Minor: the judge called 'LlamaGuard 4' appears as 'LlamaGuard2' in the methods, so the judge version is uncertain. The ablation scope is indeed unstated in the text.

statements.correction: If this study counts toward tested_with_controls: its V1 ablation has only a no-suffix baseline, with no random-direction control. There is no capability check, and Table 1 reports no uncertainty.
statements.problem: The statement is truncated, and the visible part says nothing specific about this study. The pooled counts can't be checked against this text.

statements.correction: arXiv:2607.08883 (AAAI Summer Symposia, code y), Table 1: Llama-2-7b-chat-hf, 200 steps, one universal suffix per method. Substring ASR 0.39 (no suffix) → Single 0.84, Negative 0.81, All 0.91, Layer 0.81, Token 0.76; GCG 0.76. The projection reached after optimisation is not reported.
statements.problem: The numbers come from this study's Table 1 (r4) but are credited only to 8cROPwYh3g, with that record's venue (ICLR 2026 workshop). This study is not named.

statements.correction: Table 1 LlamaGuard/HarmBench: Single 0.06/0.04, Negative 0.03/0.03, All 0.09/0.01, Layer 0.03/0.01, Token 0.00/0.00, GCG 0.00/0.00, Ablation 0.54/0.62. Substring 0.76–0.91. LlamaGuard version uncertain (Table 1 says 4, methods say 2).
statements.problem: 'Token, Layer and All essentially zero under the classifiers' conflicts with this study: All has the highest LlamaGuard score (0.09). The statement also leaves out that output-targeting GCG scores 0.00/0.00 too, so the low classifier scores are not specific to direction targeting.
Minor: GCG shows the same split (substring 0.76, classifiers 0.00/0.00), so the judge sensitivity is not specific to direction-targeted suffixes.
